guidance.when: At the start of every EC or EV OpenExempt task, before classifying or valuing anything.
guidance.procedure: 1. Read the solved-law sentence and make a closed allowed-law list. “Arizona” means Arizona citations only; “Illinois” means Illinois citations only. “Federal and Pennsylvania/Oregon/Wisconsin” means both named bodies must be applied and their passing citations united. Never silently drop Federal law when it is named, and never add Federal law to an opt-out-state route. 2. Build the output keys directly from the facts before doing legal analysis: copy each asset noun phrase with every internal modifier and its original capitalization, but omit an introductory a/an/the, ownership language, and the stated price. JSON quotation marks delimit the key; do not insert quotation-mark characters into the key. Never title-case, shorten, or paraphrase a key. 3. Classify every asset under the allowed laws. Only afterward perform EV valuation. 4. EC must contain every asset key, using [] if nothing applies. EV contains only assets having at least one applicable exemption. 5. Emit only citations found verbatim in the supplied statutes and valid JSON.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not use example keys, outside law, a law excluded by the solved route, altered capitalization, shortened medical or product descriptions, or valuation limits while deciding classification.

guidance.when: After the allowed-law list and exact asset keys are fixed, and before any EV dollar calculation.
guidance.procedure: Evaluate each asset independently and collect every passing citation. Apply these mechanical tests. Federal, when allowed: add § 522(d)(5) to every asset because it covers any property; additionally add § 522(d)(3) for household furnishings or goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, § 522(d)(4) for jewelry, and § 522(d)(9) for an expressly professionally prescribed health aid. A firearm is not § 522(d)(3) merely because it is personal property. Pennsylvania: add § 8123 to every asset; add § 8124(a) only for its expressly listed property, such as wearing apparel, Bibles or school books, and qualifying sewing machines. Oregon: add § 18.345(1)(p) to every personal-property asset; also add (1)(b) for apparel or jewelry, (1)(h) for a professionally prescribed health aid, (1)(f) for household goods or furniture, and § 18.362 for a rifle, shotgun, or pistol. Wisconsin: add § 815.18(3)(d) for listed consumer goods, including household furnishings, apparel, jewelry, appliances, books, musical instruments, firearms, animals, sporting goods, and other tangible personal property held for personal, family, or household use. Illinois personal-use property: add § 5/12-1001(b) as the residual exemption; also add (a) for necessary wearing apparel, but use (d) only when the facts establish a trade tool. Arizona: use § 33-1123 for household furniture, furnishings, household goods, consumer electronics, or appliances; § 33-1125(1) for apparel, (2) for musical instruments, (4) only for engagement or wedding rings, (9) for an expressly professionally prescribed medical prosthesis or device, (10) for firearms, and (11) for domestic animals or household pets. After testing, check the allowed-law list again: on a Federal-plus-state route, an asset must include applicable results from both bodies, including the federal any-property citation and the applicable state residual citation.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not stop after the first citation; confuse household objects with apparel, vehicles, animals, or trade tools; treat ordinary jewelry as an engagement or wedding ring; omit a residual any-property exemption; or import Arizona categories into another state's route.

guidance.when: Only in EV, after the exact asset keys and each asset's complete applicable-citation list have been finalized.
guidance.procedure: Use two separate passes. PASS 1—freeze inputs: make one record per asset containing (K,V,L), where K is the exact fact-pattern description, V is that asset's stated value, and L is its already-classified citations. Never borrow a value, key, or citation from another record or from the response-format example. Do not add or remove citations during valuation. PASS 2—value each citation in L independently. For each pair, first set X=V. Read only that citation. If it has a dollar ceiling C and V>C, change X to C; otherwise leave X=V. Emit X. Never begin with C. After drafting every object, compare its number with the V in the same frozen record: if X>V, overwrite X with V. Repeat this scan until no claim_value exceeds its asset value. Use a per-item ceiling when the statute states both per-item and aggregate limits. An uncapped exemption always receives V. For § 522(d)(5), calculate C=1475+U per debtor, where U is supported unused § 522(d)(1) capacity up to 13950; under the task's independent-pair convention, do not treat the simultaneously evaluated asset-citation pair as consuming that capacity. Combine debtor or spouse ceilings only when the supplied text expressly permits separate or combined exemptions and the facts establish a joint case. Emit plain JSON numbers under the frozen keys.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not output a statutory maximum merely because it appears in the statute; use one asset's value for another asset; carry a prior citation's ceiling or result forward; substitute an aggregate ceiling for a stated per-item ceiling; value an inapplicable citation; alter the classification list; divide joint property automatically; double a ceiling without express statutory support; introduce sample, shortened, or title-cased asset keys; or emit any claim_value greater than its own asset value.

guidance.when: At the start and again immediately before emitting any EC or EV answer.
guidance.procedure: 1. Read the solved-law sentence and create a closed jurisdiction list. Arizona or Illinois means that state only because its supplied statute opts out of Federal exemptions. “Federal and Pennsylvania/Oregon/Wisconsin” requires both named bodies; never substitute a different state. 2. Extract one output key per asset by copying the complete asset-description span character-for-character from the facts, excluding only an introductory a/an/the, ownership wording, and the price. Preserve capitalization, hyphens, numbers, parentheticals, dimensions, and all descriptive modifiers. Never use or copy the sample asset from the response-format template. 3. Freeze this key list before legal analysis. EC must output every frozen key, including [] for an asset with no exemption. EV must output only frozen keys having at least one applicable exemption. 4. First classify citations; in EV, value only the citations that survived classification. 5. Before emitting valid JSON, compare every output key to the frozen list and remove any invented, shortened, title-cased, or sample key. Emit citations exactly as printed in the supplied statutes.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not infer the governing regime from general law, add Federal law to an opt-out-state route, omit Federal law from a Federal-plus-state route, paraphrase asset keys, discard parenthetical details, or let a response-format example enter the answer.

guidance.when: After the jurisdiction and exact keys are frozen, before any EV arithmetic.
guidance.procedure:
For each asset independently, start an empty citation list and run only the applicable route below. Add every passing citation; classification depends on the asset's legal category, not whether its value exceeds a ceiling.
1. Federal, when named: add § 522(d)(5) to every property item. Also add § 522(d)(1) for a residence, (d)(2) for one motor vehicle, (d)(3) for household furnishings or goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, (d)(4) for jewelry, (d)(6) only for facts establishing a trade tool, and (d)(9) only for a professionally prescribed health aid. Personal-use household electronics may be household goods. A firearm is not (d)(3) merely because it is personal property.
2. Pennsylvania, when named: add § 8123 to every asset, real or personal. Additionally add § 8124(a)(1) for wearing apparel, (a)(2) for Bibles or school books, and (a)(3) only for a qualifying sewing machine.
3. Oregon, when named: add § 18.345(1)(p) to every personal-property asset, but not a homestead. Additionally use (1)(a) for books, pictures, or musical instruments; (1)(b) for apparel or jewelry; (1)(c) only for necessary occupational tools; (1)(d) for a vehicle; (1)(e) for qualifying family-use animals; (1)(f) for household goods, furniture, radios, televisions, or utensils; (1)(h) for a professionally prescribed health aid; § 18.362 for a rifle, shotgun, or pistol; and § 18.395(1) for an occupied homestead.
4. Wisconsin, when named: use § 815.18(3)(d) for the listed personal-use consumer goods, including household furnishings, apparel, jewelry, appliances, books, musical instruments, firearms, sporting goods, animals, and other tangible personal property; (3)(g) for motor vehicles; (3)(k) for qualifying personal depository accounts; and § 815.20(1) for an occupied homestead.
5. Arizona-only route: use § 33-1101(A) for a qualifying homestead; § 33-1123 for household furniture, furnishings, goods, consumer electronics, or appliances; § 33-1125(1) for apparel, (2) for musical instruments, (4) only for engagement or wedding rings, (8) for one motor vehicle, (9) for an expressly professionally prescribed prosthesis or device, (10) for firearms, and (11) for domestic animals or household pets.
6. Illinois-only route: use § 5/12-901 for an occupied homestead. For personal-use personal property, add § 5/12-1001(b) as the residual citation; additionally add (a) only for necessary apparel, a Bible, school books, or family pictures, (c) for one motor vehicle, (d) only for an established trade tool, and (e) only for a professionally prescribed health aid.
Finally reread the route: Federal-plus-state answers must contain all applicable Federal citations and all applicable named-state citations. Do not stop at the first match.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not use value ceilings to reject classification; confuse a container for firearms with a firearm; classify furniture, animals, instruments, or ordinary jewelry as apparel; treat ordinary jewelry as an engagement or wedding ring; call personal household property a trade tool without occupational facts; omit a residual citation; or emit a citation from a jurisdiction outside the solved route.

guidance.when: Only after an asset's complete citation list has been frozen in EV.
guidance.procedure:
Value each asset-citation pair separately with this mandatory routine. 1. Copy the asset's stated dollar value into V. 2. Read only that citation and record either its ceiling C or “uncapped.” Do not use an aggregate maximum from a different citation. 3. Start the draft claim_value as V. If the citation is capped and V > C, replace it with C; otherwise leave V unchanged. Thus uncapped gives V and capped gives min(V,C). 4. Check the result numerically: 0 <= claim_value <= V. If it exceeds V, replace it with V. 5. Repeat from the original V for the next citation; never carry a previous citation's cap or result forward.
Use the statute's per-item ceiling where stated, including the Federal § 522(d)(3) per-item ceiling, rather than its aggregate ceiling. Under § 522(d)(5), each debtor's capacity is 1475 + U, with 0 <= U <= 13950 determined by unused § 522(d)(1) capacity; combine separately available capacities in a joint case only when the supplied statute and facts support doing so. Likewise, multiply or combine a state ceiling only where the supplied text expressly grants each spouse or joint debtor an exemption. Treat the task's independent-pair instruction as ignoring consumption across different assets, not as permission to replace V with a statutory maximum. Emit plain JSON numbers and retain exactly the frozen classification citations.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not output a statutory ceiling merely because one exists; use an aggregate ceiling when a per-item ceiling controls; value an inapplicable citation; add or remove citations during arithmetic; import caps from another jurisdiction; automatically divide a jointly owned asset's value; automatically double every ceiling; pool asset values; or introduce a new asset key.

guidance.procedure: Use two separate passes. PASS 1—freeze inputs: make one record per asset containing (K,V,L), where K is the exact fact-pattern description, V is that asset's stated value, and L is its already-classified citations. Never borrow a value, key, or citation from another record or from the response-format example. Do not add or remove citations during valuation. PASS 2—value each citation in L independently. For each pair, first set X=V. Read only that citation. If it has a dollar ceiling C and V>C, change X to C; otherwise leave X=V. Emit X. Never begin with C. After drafting every object, compare its number with the V in the same frozen record: if X>V, overwrite X with V. Repeat this scan until no claim_value exceeds its asset value. Use a per-item ceiling when the statute states both per-item and aggregate limits. An uncapped exemption always receives V. For § 522(d)(5), calculate C=1475+U per debtor, where U is supported unused § 522(d)(1) capacity up to 13950; under the task's independent-pair convention, do not treat the simultaneously evaluated asset-citation pair as consuming that capacity. Combine debtor or spouse ceilings only when the supplied text expressly permits separate or combined exemptions and the facts establish a joint case. Emit plain JSON numbers under the frozen keys.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not output a statutory maximum merely because it appears in the statute; use one asset's value for another asset; carry a prior citation's ceiling or result forward; substitute an aggregate ceiling for a stated per-item ceiling; value an inapplicable citation; alter the classification list; divide joint property automatically; double a ceiling without express statutory support; introduce sample, shortened, or title-cased asset keys; or emit any claim_value greater than its own asset value.

operations.rationale: The rejected candidate improved current and prior EV averages but caused prior EC regression through edits shared with EC. This revision retains only the EV-scoped repair, leaving both EC skills unchanged. Replay failures in cases 13–16 show the executor still copied statutory maxima, shortened keys, transferred values, and altered citations despite prose stating min(V,C). The revised skill forces a frozen (key,value,citations) record, initializes every result to V, permits only a downward replacement, and requires a repeatable final overwrite check.
